html:
The mosque of Mehmed II, "the Conqueror" (Fatih), built from 1463 to 1470 in Istanbul, ten years after the fall of Constantinople. It stands on the site of the Church of the Holy Apostles, the burial church of Byzantine emperors since Constantine, which was already derelict and was pulled down to make room. Its architect was the Greek Atik Sinan. It was the first great project of Ottoman imperial architecture in the city.

The mosque sat in a complex of unprecedented size, about 325 m on each side: eight madrasas, the Sahn-ı Seman, which taught some thousand students theology, law, medicine and astronomy, with a library, a hospital, a guesthouse, a caravanserai, a bath, a school, a kitchen for the poor and 280 shops. The first mosque had a dome 26 m wide backed by a single half dome toward Mecca. Earthquakes damaged it in 1509, 1557 and 1754, and the earthquake of 22 May 1766 brought the dome down.

Sultan Mustafa III had it rebuilt from 1767 to 1771 by Mehmet Tahir Ağa on a new plan, a central dome with four half domes like the Şehzade Mosque. Only the courtyard, the main gate, the mihrab and the lower parts of the minarets are original. Mehmed II and his consort Gülbahar lie in tombs in the garden behind; new sultans came here to visit the Conqueror's tomb after being girded with the Sword of Osman at Eyüp. The madrasas still flank the mosque on both sides.
